chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 351 to 360, Othalanthaiyar's paalai decade on the return (வரவுரைத்த பத்து): the friend tells the wife that the men who crossed the waste have come back, and the man himself tells her that thinking of her he gave up the wealth-quest, and that the long burnt road grew short and easy on the way home.

351.reading: The friend tells the woman that the men have come back, leaving behind them the wasteland where travellers on the hard road eat the small sun-scorched fruit of the desert jackfruit and pass on, so the withered state of her lovely waist may now be cured.
351.nuance: The road is measured by its food: the only meal it offers is a fruit the sun has already eaten (வெயில்தின்), so the men's return is set against a land that half-consumes whatever is in it, as separation had wasted her body.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard road under a sun that eats the fruit fixes the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வரவுரைத்த பத்து, poems telling of the return); the friend tells the woman, whom she addresses (மடந்தை நின்), that the men have come

352.reading: Our lover has come back, says the speaker to her friend, without calling hard the burning waste where the great-trunked elephant, its hide ridged like the lettered hero-stone of men who fell to the arrows of strong-bowed warriors, vents its dark rage.
352.nuance: The hero-stone, the waste's sign of men killed on the road, enters only as the likeness of a living elephant's hide, so the danger is doubled while the poem's point stays that the man did not count it (அரிய என்னார). Lines 1 and 2 repeat a formula of Akananuru 53.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot waste road is the land of the poem

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வரவுரைத்த பத்து, poems telling of the return); the vocative தோழி with நம் காதலோர் would also fit the woman speaking to her friend; the decade's title favours the friend announcing the return

353.reading: The men who crossed the hills of great dark groves have come back, so that she may sweetly embrace that beautiful raised chest on which bright ornaments shine like a red hill encircled by a creeper of flame.
353.nuance: The image gives the returning man's chest the look of a hill, the very thing he crossed: the land he left her for comes back to her as the body she embraces. எரிக்கொடி may be a red-flowered creeper or a line of fire; either way the basis is colour.

thinai_evidence.note: the men who crossed the hills return to end the separation

comparisons.tenor: his broad chest with its shining ornaments

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வரவுரைத்த பத்து, poems telling of the return); the friend tells the woman (நீ இனிது முயங்க) that the men have come

354.reading: The friend tells the woman that he has crossed back over the hard road where the red wild-dog, having mated with its tender female, passes by the doe with her fawn without seizing her, hurrying because her nature drew him.
354.nuance: The predator of the waste, which in other paalai poems kills on the road, here holds back: the beasts the man passed on the way home already show the restraint and tenderness he is bringing back.

thinai_evidence.note: the hard waste road of the wild dog

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வரவுரைத்த பத்து, poems telling of the return); the friend addresses the woman (தெரியிழை அரிவை நின்)

iraicchi.act: the male wild dog, keeping to its mate, lets the doe with her fawn go unharmed
iraicchi.sense: a beast at one with its mate spares another's mother and young, as the man, drawn by his wife, left off his own seizing of wealth and hurried home

355.reading: The man tells his wife that, thinking of her beauty, he turned back without so much as saying 'may the hard work of the wealth-quest win great fortune', from the forest whose tracks cross the path and where small-eyed elephants with spotted faces roam.
355.nuance: He abandons the wealth-quest without even the courtesy of a blessing on it: the omitted farewell (சொல்லாது) is the measure of how completely her beauty outweighed the project.

thinai_evidence.note: the man gives up the journey for wealth and comes back

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வரவுரைத்த பத்து, poems telling of the return); the man speaks of himself to the woman (திருந்திழை அரிவை, நின்னலம்)

356.reading: The man tells his wife that her virtues are truly sweet to think of, for in the waste that bright fire has grazed over they drew his heart back like the gold-worked rope with which rich men tie their elephant.
356.nuance: The comparison is made by the case ending of கயிற்றின், not by அன்ன or போல. The rope is costly as well as strong: what pulls him home is fine and precious, and he is the great beast that it holds.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வரவுரைத்த பத்து, poems telling of the return); the man addresses the woman (நின் குணனே)

357.reading: Our lover has come back, the friend tells the woman: seeing the forest dressed for the season, kuravam opening and maravam in flower, he said 'let the journey for wealth be given up' and came, longing for her, so that her lovely dark glowing skin may regain its beauty.
357.nuance: The flowering that usually marks a promised season of return here works on the man himself: the forest he was crossing put on its adornment (அணி) and reminded him of his own wife's beauty, so he turned back mid-journey.

thinai_evidence.note: the man gives up the journey on seeing the season

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வரவுரைத்த பத்து, poems telling of the return); as in 352 the vocative தோழி could also make the woman the speaker

358.reading: Though he has crossed many high-peaked hills, will her eyes let him stay away long, eyes that, thinking long of him, cloud over each time they are wiped and have become a flood that bursts out?
358.nuance: The subject of நீடவிடுமோ is the eyes: the tears are imagined as a force that will not allow his delay, so grief itself becomes the pledge of his return.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone beyond the hills and is waited for

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வரவுரைத்த பத்து, poems telling of the return); the speaker is not named; the third-person இறந்தனர் and the assurance that he cannot stay long fit the friend comforting the woman, but the woman speaking of her own eyes is also possible

359.reading: The man tells his wife that when he left her, wanting rare wealth, and parted on the rocky tracks, the ways through the waste were very long, but now, as he comes thinking of her, they have become near.
359.nuance: The same road has two lengths: going out for wealth it stretched, coming back for her it shrank, so distance is made a property of desire, not of the land.

thinai_evidence.note: going for wealth and coming back

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வரவுரைத்த பத்து, poems telling of the return); the man addresses the woman (அணியிழை)

360.reading: The man tells his doe-eyed wife that the long way through the summer heat, whose growth fire has seized and eaten, though hard, was easy when he drove his swift-horsed sturdy chariot, his aching heart longing for her embrace, thinking of her as he came.
360.nuance: மான் occurs twice in two lines with two senses, the swift horse he drives and the deer whose look is hers: the creature that carries him and the creature she resembles meet in the last two lines.

thinai_evidence.note: the long summer road scorched by fire

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade (வரவுரைத்த பத்து, poems telling of the return); the man addresses the woman (நெடுமான் நோக்கி நின்)

links.note: Ainkurunuru 355: he turned back from the wealth journey without blessing it; Akananuru 337: the heart once said 'let wealth stay there' (அவணதாகப் பொருள்) and came back alone, and now presses for a second journey.
links.teaches: Akananuru 337 supplies the sequel the Ainkurunuru decade leaves out: the return for love that 355 presents as final is, a season later, reopened by the same heart, so the turning back is one move in a recurring quarrel between wealth and the wife.

links.note: In Akananuru 97 the kuravam blooms (குரவுமலர்ந்து) in a spring when the man has not come and the woman cannot stop her tears; in Ainkurunuru 357 the kuravam's flowering is what makes the man give up his journey.
links.teaches: Held together, the two poems show the spring flowers acting on both lovers at once: the same blossoming that tortures the waiting woman in Akananuru 97 is, in 357, what turns the man back, so the season's sign has power over him and fails only when he ignores it.

links.note: In Natrinai 43 a starving red dog kills a weary wild cow on the road the man is about to take; in Ainkurunuru 354 the red dog, with its mate, lets the doe with her fawn go on the road he has taken home.
links.teaches: The same predator of the waste kills on the outbound road and holds back on the homeward one, so the paalai poets set the beast's act to the direction of the journey: cruelty when the man leaves, restraint when he comes back to his wife.

links.note: Both use the formula விழுத்தொடை மறவர் வில் இட ... எழுத்துடை நடுகல்; in Akananuru 53 it is the stone on the outbound road the woman says he chose over her, in Ainkurunuru 352 a simile for an elephant on the road he did not call hard on his way back.
links.teaches: The one formula of the lettered hero-stone serves opposite arguments: in Akananuru 53 the woman reads the deadly road as proof he loves wealth more than her, while 352 makes the same road proof of love because he crossed it home without counting its danger.

links.note: In Kural 1170 the woman says her eyes would not swim in a flood of tears if they could go to him as her heart does; in Ainkurunuru 358 the eyes, which have become a flood however often they are wiped, will not let him stay away long.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the flood of tears a sign of the eyes' helplessness, bound to the house while the heart travels, whereas the Sangam poem turns that same flood into a power that pulls him back, so the tears are complaint in one and pledge of return in the other.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 360: the long burnt road was easy because he drove his chariot thinking of her; Akananuru 9: the returning man's heart outran even his sleepless chariot and has already reached her.
links.teaches: Read together the two returns show desire working on the journey in two stages: in 360 it shrinks the road the chariot must cover, and in Akananuru 9 it leaves the chariot behind altogether, so the heart arrives before the man does.

source_issues.issue: The word உடிஅத்தெழு is not a regular form; the sense (a flood that breaks out) suggests உடைத்தெழு. Marked uncertain; the word is not used as evidence.
The colophon has no thurai for any poem of this decade; speakers in thurai_akam are inferred from the poems.
